segments.say: Lesson 12. Monolith versus Microservices. A P I gateway, service discovery, service mesh, data ownership and when N O T to split.

A monolith is one big application deployed as a unit. Microservices split it into small independent services, each owning one business area and its own data, talking over the network. Here is an analogy. One big department store (monolith) versus a mall of specialist shops (microservices): the shops open and renovate independently, but you need corridors, signs and security between them.

Why does this matter? "Monolith or microservices?" is a frequent trade-off question. A few key words. Service: Independently deployable component. A P I gateway: The single front door for clients. Service discovery: How services find each other. Saga: Multi-service transaction with compensating steps.
Microservices architecture. An A P I gateway is the single front door: authentication, rate limiting, request routing, and aggregation for clients.
Each service owns one business capability and is deployed and scaled independently by its own team.
Database per service: no shared tables. Others go through the A P I or events, never the D B directly.
Sync calls (rest/G R P C) for immediate needs. Each call adds latency and a failure point, so use timeouts, retries and circuit breakers.
Async events (OrderPlaced) let other services react without tight coupling.
Plus service discovery (Consul, Kubernetes D N S), a service mesh (Istio/Linkerd for mTLS, retries, telemetry), and distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry). Powerful, but it's operational overhead.

Honest trade-offs. Monolith: one deployable. Simple to build, test and debug; transactions are easy. Pain arrives with large teams (merge conflicts, slow deploys, all-or-nothing scaling). Microservices: team autonomy, independent deploy and scale, fault isolation, tech freedom. Costs: network latency, distributed data consistency (sagas), observability, infrastructure complexity. Modular monolith: clean internal module boundaries in one deployable. A great default that's easy to split later.

Distributed data. No cross-service acid transactions. Use sagas: a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions (refund if shipping fails). C Q R S: separate write model from read model (materialized views fed by events). Accept eventual consistency between services.

Say it in the interview. "I'd start with a modular monolith unless team size or scaling needs justify microservices. When splitting, I follow business capabilities with database-per-service, an A P I gateway in front, G R P C or rest for sync calls with timeouts and circuit breakers, events for async workflows, sagas instead of distributed transactions, and OpenTelemetry tracing across everything.".

Let's compare. Deploy: all together, independently. Scaling: whole app, per service. Data: one D B, acid, D B per service, eventual consistency. Latency: in-process calls, network hops. Debugging: stack trace, distributed tracing. Team fit: small teams, many autonomous teams.

A likely interview question: When would you N O T use microservices? A strong answer: Small team, early product, unclear domain boundaries, or no platform or observability maturity. A modular monolith gives most of the benefits with far less operational cost.
That's it for Monolith versus Microservices. Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
